title: Erdős Problem #931: Same Prime Factors in Products of Consecutive Integers
description: Let k₁ ≥ k₂ ≥ 3. Are there only finitely many n₂ ≥ n₁+k₁ such that ∏(n₁+i) and ∏(n₂+j) share the same prime factors? Counterexamples to the stronger claim exist (AlphaProof: 10! and 14·15·16). OPEN.

meta.author: Erdős
meta.assumptions: 2 sorry-stated assumptions (theorem-with-sorry, formerly axioms): stronger_implies_main (Størmer-type smooth number argument), exists_prime_between_blocks_hard (refined: only the hard case with k₁<n₁, tight gap, all factors ≤n₁ — general statement proved as theorem). overview.historicalContext: Erdős posed this problem in 1976 [Er76d], asking about the finiteness of pairs of consecutive-integer blocks whose products share the same set of prime factors. The problem appears in Guy's _Unsolved Problems in Number Theory_ as Problem B35. The question connects to deep themes in multiplicative number theory: the radical $\text{rad}(n)$ (product of distinct prime factors) of a product $(n+1)\cdots(n+k) = (n+k)!/n!$ depends on which primes $\leq n+k$ divide at least one element of the block. Erdős himself doubted the full conjecture and proposed the weaker claim that same-prime-factor pairs must satisfy $n_2 > 2(n_1 + k_1)$ with finitely many exceptions. This stronger conjecture was disproved by a counterexample: $10! = 2^8 \cdot 3^4 \cdot 5^2 \cdot 7$ and $14 \cdot 15 \cdot 16 = 2^5 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdot 7$ share prime factors $\{2,3,5,7\}$ with $n_2 = 13 \leq 20 = 2(n_1 + k_1)$. Tijdeman found another example: $19 \cdot 20 \cdot 21 \cdot 22$ and $54 \cdot 55 \cdot 56 \cdot 57$ share the same primes (this one beyond the double gap). The connection to Bertrand's postulate is central: for $n_2 > 2(n_1 + k_1)$, a prime in $(n_1 + k_1, 2(n_1 + k_1)]$ would divide the second block but not the first, reducing the problem to the bounded-gap case. The constraint $k_1, k_2 \geq 3$ excludes trivial infinite families for small block sizes.
overview.problemStatement: Let $k_1 \geq k_2 \geq 3$. Are there only finitely many $n_2 \geq n_1 + k_1$ such that $\prod_{i=1}^{k_1}(n_1+i)$ and $\prod_{j=1}^{k_2}(n_2+j)$ have the same set of prime factors?
overview.text: Let k₁ ≥ k₂ ≥ 3. Are there only finitely many n₂ ≥ n₁+k₁ such that ∏(n₁+i) and ∏(n₂+j) share the same prime factors? Counterexamples to the stronger claim exist (AlphaProof: 10! and 14·15·16). OPEN.
overview.proofStrategy: The formalization defines `consecutiveProduct` via `Finset.Icc` and `Finset.prod`, extracts prime factor sets via `Nat.primeFactors`, and defines `SamePrimeFactors` as equality of these Finsets. The main conjecture uses `Set.Finite` on the solution set. Both the stronger conjecture ($n_2 \leq 2(n_1+k_1)$) and the prime-between-blocks question are stated as theorem-with-sorry (formerly axioms; converted for axiom-integrity). Two counterexamples (AlphaProof and Tijdeman) are fully verified by `native_decide` and `omega`. Structural properties (positivity, prime factor membership, equivalence relation) are proved. The file uses 2 sorry statements; the deep results are sorry-stated theorems.
keyInsights: AlphaProof counterexample: $10!$ and $14 \cdot 15 \cdot 16$ share prime factors $\{2,3,5,7\}$ with $n_2 \leq 2(n_1+k_1)$, disproving the stronger conjecture
Tijdeman's example: $19 \cdot 20 \cdot 21 \cdot 22$ and $54 \cdot 55 \cdot 56 \cdot 57$ share primes but with $n_2 > 2(n_1+k_1)$, so the original finiteness question persists
Bertrand's postulate reduces the problem: for $n_2 > 2(n_1+k_1)$, a prime in $(n_1+k_1, 2(n_1+k_1)]$ provides a distinguishing factor, so only the bounded-gap case matters
The constraint $k_1, k_2 \geq 3$ is essential: for $k = 1$ or $k = 2$, infinitely many pairs trivially share prime factors (e.g., all even consecutive products share the prime 2)
Erdős could not prove even the subsidiary question: must a prime exist between $n_1$ and $n_2 + k_2$ when the blocks share prime factors?
The `SamePrimeFactors` relation is an equivalence relation on $(n, k)$ pairs, suggesting a quotient structure that could organize the solution space

sections.title: Verified Counterexamples
sections.summary: Five verified examples: AlphaProof (n₁=0, k₁=10, n₂=13, k₂=3), Tijdeman (n₁=18, k₁=k₂=4, n₂=53), and three new small examples showing {4,5,6}/{8,9,10}, {3,4,5,6}/{8,9,10}, and {1..5}/{8,9,10} share prime factors {2,3,5}. All verified by native_decide and omega.

sections.title: Properties of Prime Factors
sections.summary: Seven lemmas: prime factors divide the product and are prime, a prime dividing any n+i is in the factor set (via Finset.dvd_prod_of_mem), and SamePrimeFactors is reflexive, symmetric, transitive.

sections.title: Bertrand's Postulate and Prime Between Blocks
sections.summary: NEW: Four theorems using Bertrand's postulate. (1) If the first block contains a prime, a prime exists in range (trivial). (2) By Bertrand, when k₁ ≥ n₁ the first block always has a prime. (3) Combined: exists_prime_between_blocks holds for k₁ ≥ n₁ without SamePrimeFactors. (4) If the first product has a large prime factor, SamePrimeFactors transfers it to bound q ≤ n₂+k₂ via Prime.dvd_finset_prod_iff.
sections.mathContext: NEW: Four theorems using Bertrand's postulate. (1) If the first block contains a prime, a prime exists in range (trivial). (2) By Bertrand, when k₁ ≥ n₁ the first block always has a prime. (3) Combined: exists_prime_between_blocks holds for k₁ ≥ n₁ without SamePrimeFactors.

sections.title: Prime Between Blocks: Proved from Refined Axiom
sections.summary: The general exists_prime_between_blocks statement is a THEOREM proved by 4-way case analysis: (1) k₁≥n₁ via Bertrand, (2) n₂+k₂≥2n₁ via Bertrand, (3) large prime factor transfer via SamePrimeFactors, (4) the refined hard case (k₁<n₁, tight gap, all factors ≤n₁) discharged by exists_prime_between_blocks_hard, a theorem-with-sorry (formerly axiom) strictly weaker than the original with 3 additional constraining hypotheses.
sections.mathContext: The general exists_prime_between_blocks statement is proved by 4-way case analysis. Only the hard case (k₁<n₁, n₂+k₂<2n₁, all prime factors ≤n₁) remains a sorry-stated theorem. This case forces both blocks to be n₁-smooth, making it likely vacuously true by Størmer-type results.

sections.title: Structural Lemmas
sections.summary: After 'Problem Status' and 'Structural Lemmas' markers: exists_multiple_in_block (among k consecutive integers, one is divisible by any d ≤ k), prime_le_k_mem_factors (every prime p ≤ k is a prime factor of the block product), and two_mem_factors (2 is a factor when k ≥ 2). Proved via division/modular arithmetic and omega.
sections.mathContext: Mathematical content: exists_multiple_in_block (among k consecutive integers, one is divisible by any d ≤ k), prime_le_k_mem_factors (every prime p ≤ k is a prime factor of the block product), and two_mem_factors. Proved via division/modular arithmetic and omega.

sections.title: Hard Case Structure: Both Blocks Are Entirely Composite
sections.summary: In the hard case (k₁<n₁, n₂+k₂<2n₁, all prime factors ≤n₁), four theorems show both blocks consist entirely of composites: hard_case_first_block_composite, hard_case_second_block_composite (via SamePrimeFactors), hard_case_second_block_smooth (every prime factor of the second product ≤n₁), and hard_case_summary collecting all structural constraints.
sections.mathContext: Mathematical content: hard_case_first_block_composite, hard_case_second_block_composite (via SamePrimeFactors), hard_case_second_block_smooth, and hard_case_summary. Both blocks are forced to be n₁-smooth composites, the core structural constraint of the hard case.

sections.title: Hard Case: Lower Bound on n₁
sections.summary: The hard-case constraints k₁<n₁, k₁≥k₂≥3, n₁+k₁≤n₂, and n₂+k₂<2n₁ force n₁≥k₁+k₂+1≥7. hard_case_n1_lower_bound and hard_case_n2_range (the valid range [n₁+k₁, 2n₁−k₂−1] for n₂ is non-empty), both by omega.
sections.mathContext: Mathematical content: hard_case_n1_lower_bound (n₁ ≥ k₁+k₂+1 ≥ 7) and hard_case_n2_range (valid n₂ range [n₁+k₁, 2n₁−k₂−1] is non-empty), both discharged by omega.

sections.title: Hard Case: No Prime in First Block
sections.summary: Since all prime factors of the first product are ≤n₁, there is no prime in {n₁+1,...,n₁+k₁}: hard_case_no_prime_in_first_block derives False from a prime in the block, and hard_case_next_prime_beyond_block concludes the next prime after n₁ must exceed n₁+k₁.
sections.mathContext: Mathematical content: hard_case_no_prime_in_first_block (a prime in the first block contradicts h₇) and hard_case_next_prime_beyond_block (the next prime after n₁ exceeds n₁+k₁). Combined with Bertrand this places the next prime in (n₁+k₁, 2n₁].

sections.title: Hard Case: Computational Verification for Small n₁
sections.summary: hard_case_vacuous_k3_n30: for k₁=k₂=3 and n₁∈[7,30], no valid hard-case instance exists — for every n₂∈[n₁+3, 2n₁−4] either the first block has a prime factor >n₁ or SamePrimeFactors fails. Proved by native_decide, giving empirical evidence the hard case is vacuously true.
sections.mathContext: Mathematical content: hard_case_vacuous_k3_n30 verifies via native_decide that for k₁=k₂=3 and n₁∈[7,30] the hard-case hypotheses are never simultaneously satisfiable, evidence that the remaining sorry-stated hard case is vacuously true.

conclusion.summary: Erdős Problem #931 asks whether two far-apart blocks of consecutive integers can share the same set of prime factors only finitely often. The formalization defines the core objects (`consecutiveProduct`, `consecutivePrimeFactors`, `SamePrimeFactors`), states the main finiteness conjecture and its stronger variant, and fully verifies two counterexamples to the stronger claim. Seven structural lemmas are proved (including the equivalence relation property), and the Bertrand's postulate reduction and prime-between-blocks question are recorded as theorem-with-sorry (formerly axioms; converted for axiom-integrity). The file uses 2 sorry statements.
conclusion.implications: Resolution would illuminate the multiplicative structure of consecutive integers at a deep level: how far apart can blocks be while sharing the exact same prime support? The connection to Bertrand's postulate and prime gaps means progress could come from improved bounds on prime distribution in structured intervals. The problem also connects to the abc conjecture (which constrains radical sizes in additive relations) and to Grimm's conjecture (which requires distinct prime factors for consecutive composite numbers).
openQuestions: Are there only finitely many pairs $(n_1, n_2)$ with same prime factors for fixed $k_1 \geq k_2 \geq 3$? The main conjecture remains completely open.
Must a prime exist between $n_1$ and $n_2 + k_2$ when blocks share prime factors? Even this seemingly weaker consequence is unproved.
What is the growth rate of the largest $n_2$ with $\text{SamePrimeFactors}(n_1, k_1, n_2, k_2)$ as a function of $n_1$ and $k$?
Are there infinitely many counterexamples to the stronger conjecture ($n_2 \leq 2(n_1+k_1)$), or is the AlphaProof example essentially isolated?
How does the problem change if we require not just the same prime factor set but the same prime factorization signature (same multiset of exponents)?
